A set of both equimolar and non-equimolar HECs are predicted to be stable in order to further synthesize those compositions based on the predictions.

papers.title: Generalizing and Combining Check Constructions: Design-Space Exploration for Fault-Tolerant Quantum State Preparation
papers.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing needs logical states prepared such that single faults cannot spread into uncorrectable errors. Post-selection achieves this with added checks that detect dangerous faults and discard the run. How the checks are measured sets the depth and operation count of the circuit, and the best trade-off depends on the hardware. Existing automated methods, however, each use one check construction and yield fixed trade-offs.   We first introduce Block Checks, in which several checks share one fault-tolerantly prepared auxiliary block, which places them and existing constructions in a single design space. Second, to explore that space, we propose a Pareto tree search that adds checks and auxiliary blocks, merges auxiliaries, and edits the circuit. On quantum codes of distance up to seven, the search finds best-known circuits for many new operation--depth trade-offs and surpasses existing methods. The code is open source as part of the Munich Quantum Toolkit (MQT) at https://github.com/munich-quantum-toolkit/qecc, and all circuits are available in the QECirc library at https://qecirc.com.

papers.title: A measurement-free quantum error correction protocol for superconducting cavities
papers.abstract: The realization of large-scale quantum computation will require quantum error correction (QEC). One way to reduce the demands placed on QEC is to correct dominant physical errors at a lower level before passing the remaining errors to an outer code. Recently, Krastanov et al. [Nat. Commun. 12, 191 (2021)] proposed a measurement-free error-correction protocol based on coherent control of photonic modes that corrects for photon loss. Here, we adapt this approach to a circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED) architecture using three superconducting microwave cavities coupled by Josephson-junction-based nonlinear elements. We encode the logical qubit in the lowest-order binomial code of one cavity, while the two other cavities serve as ancillas. Using numerical simulations with experimentally realistic parameters, we demonstrate that our protocol can correct single-photon loss with 99% fidelity. Furthermore, we optimize the waiting time between successive rounds of error-correction, and show that the logical lifetime can be extended by a factor of 1.2-1.8 relative to the unprotected Fock $\{|0\rangle, |1\rangle\}$ encoding, surpassing break-even performance. Our work highlights the potential of gate-based, measurement-free QEC for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

papers.title: BuggyMLE: Scaling Machine Learning Engineering Difficulty with Bug Injection
papers.abstract: Enabling AI systems to autonomously improve AI models requires agents capable of performing machine learning engineering (MLE). In practice, designing, training, and evaluating complex models demands modifying multi-file repositories to reproduce results, debug training runs, integrate datasets, and port frameworks. However, existing MLE benchmarks limit agents to single-file edits without full repository or shell access, and common repository-level software engineering benchmarks have rapidly saturated. To address this, we introduce the Code Complexity Index (CCI), a difficulty metric based on ten structural features spanning repository scale, dependency depth, and patch size. CCI strongly predicts average solve rates across eight public coding benchmarks ($R^2 = 0.951$), identifying patch size and complexity as top predictors. Guided by CCI, we develop BuggyMLE, a scalable framework where agents inject controlled mutations into working ML repositories, synthesizing over 6,600 bug-injected MLE repository variants and nearly 260K lines of injected code based on 222 source repositories. Using BuggyMLE, we make two contributions. First, we construct BuggyMLE-Bench-Lite, the first difficulty-graded, repository-level variant of MLE-Bench Lite; across 14 evaluated models, the top solve rate drops from 95% to 9% as difficulty is scaled from the easiest to the hardest tier. Second, we synthesize a training curriculum across three difficulty levels over 200 additional ML repositories, fine-tuning a Qwen3.5-9B model to rival frontier models on BuggyMLE-Bench-Lite. Our trained model transfers beyond ML, raising its SWE-bench Lite resolve rate from 24% to 33% and its LiveCodeBench v6 pass@1 from 69% to 71%.

papers.title: ShEPhERD-score: Fast, adaptable three-dimensional alignment of molecular features
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) molecular similarity scoring and alignment are widely employed in ligand-based virtual screening and molecular design, and are increasingly used for training and evaluating machine learning models. Existing open-source methods utilize various molecular representations spanning shape, electrostatics, pharmacophores, and hybrid representations, but their implementations as independent software packages with distinct application programming interfaces (APIs), optimizers, and limited GPU support make them difficult to compare, combine, or extend. Here, we develop ShEPhERD-score into a unified, modular platform for differentiable 3D molecular similarity scoring and alignment by combining diverse molecular representations with high-performance Numba CPU and Triton GPU kernels to support both large-scale library screening and pairwise similarity workflows. In matched comparisons with open-source 3D similarity tools on the DUDE-Z virtual screening benchmark, ShEPhERD-score performed comparably or better in eight of nine cases. Across the scoring modes in ShEPhERD-score, throughput ranges from 17,800 to 1.03 million alignments/second for ten-million-conformer libraries using a single NVIDIA L40S GPU. Moreover, we found that the most effective scoring mode varied by protein target, indicating that target-specific calibration against validation data may be valuable before large-scale screening and underscoring the need for a unified platform that provides diverse molecular representations. Together, these capabilities establish ShEPhERD-score as a single, extensible toolkit for rapid virtual screening and machine learning workflows.

papers.title: Evaluation of machine-learning and deep-learning SPEI drought forecasts against persistence across timescales and lead times in Bangladesh
papers.abstract: Bangladesh, home to nearly 178 million people, is highly vulnerable to recurring droughts that threaten food security and rural livelihoods. Machine-learning and deep-learning models are increasingly used to forecast drought indices such as the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI). Most studies report accuracy without a persistence reference, although accumulated indices are strongly autocorrelated, and seldom test drought detection, longer leads or variation between training runs. This study forecast SPEI at 3-, 6- and 12-month timescales one to three months ahead for the eight divisions of Bangladesh, using ERA5 reanalysis checked against 35 Bangladesh Meteorological Department stations. Five models, XGBoost, CNN, Bi-LSTM, CNN-BiLSTM and CEEMDAN-BiLSTM, were trained with five seeds each, scored on accuracy, skill against persistence and drought detection, and interpreted with Shapley values. At a one-month lead, the CNN-BiLSTM and Bi-LSTM beat persistence clearly at SPEI-3 and SPEI-6 (skill 0.408 and 0.350), while at SPEI-12 a Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.872 barely exceeded persistence (0.850). Skill and detection could disagree: at SPEI-3 and a three-month lead, XGBoost had the highest skill (0.439) yet detected none of the 119 drought months. Only at SPEI-6 did the forecasts beat persistence significantly and match its detection at all three leads, with fewer false alarms. At SPEI-12, gains were small or absent and varied between seeds. The forecasts kept 76-80% of their correlation against station-derived SPEI and relied mainly on precipitation and lagged SPEI. Forecasts should therefore be judged on skill against persistence and detection across several seeds, not on accuracy alone. In Bangladesh, SPEI-6 forecasts can support early warning up to three months ahead and SPEI-3 forecasts one month ahead, while SPEI-12 is better suited to monitoring.

papers.title: Unified Law for Visual Tasks (The Four Laws of Computer Vision)
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose a Unified Law for Visual Tasks, which could be further divided into Four Laws of Computer Vision, with the goal of enabling a single framework or method to uniformly train on and perform nearly all visual tasks. Our starting point is an inspiration and hypothesis: if the world information is encoded into image, which we call World Snapshots, then image processing is world processing, and image generation is World Snapshot generation. Furthermore, if all visual and visualization tasks can be reformulated as generation tasks, then a unified method, World Snapshot Models (WSMs), can perform the vast majority of visual tasks, much as large language models have largely unified natural language processing. This paper validates these laws across more than 1,000 trained and evaluated visual tasks (defined by distinct input-output mappings) and presents a unified training framework for future visual-task research and applications.

papers.title: Quantum Simulation of First-Quantised Chemistry with a Sum-of-Squares Representation
papers.abstract: Calculating molecular energies is expected to be an important application of quantum computers, but the most efficient algorithms to achieve this typically have significant space requirements. Scaling quantum processors to thousands of logical qubits is a daunting engineering challenge, so developing algorithms that run with reduced qubit requirements is of particular importance. Moreover, most algorithms are benchmarked on active spaces with about as many orbitals as electrons, missing dynamical correlation which is necessary to describe real chemistry. Capturing this correlation requires several times more orbitals than electrons, even in compact atomic-orbital basis sets. This low-filling regime favours first quantisation, where each electron is represented by a number of qubits that grows only logarithmically with the number of orbitals. Whether this approach translates into a practical advantage in orbital basis sets of realistic size, however, has been unclear. Here, we develop a first-quantised phase estimation algorithm for generic orbital basis sets, based on a non-convex sum-of-squares representation of the Hamiltonian and spectral-gap amplification. We compare it with the state-of-the-art second-quantised algorithm, compiling both with the same techniques at the logical level. For six molecules with 4 to 24 electrons in 5 to 14 times as many orbitals, our first-quantised method needs up to 16 times fewer Toffoli gates than the second-quantised algorithm in the low-qubit regime, where only a few hundred logical qubits are available. It stays cheaper up to between several hundred and about 1\,400 qubits, and its smallest qubit count is 1.4 to 2 times lower than in second quantisation. In the low-qubit and low-filling regime, our algorithm is therefore the method of choice for chemistry in orbital basis sets.

papers.title: On the Impact of Feature Reduction Techniques on Adversarial Attacks
papers.abstract: Adversarial attacks have posed significant threats to machine learning models by exploiting their inherent vulnerabilities. Researchers have established an interdisciplinary field called adversarial machine learning to explore these vulnerabilities and develop corresponding defense strategies. Feature reduction strategies are used to decrease the dimensionality of the data in order to reduce training time, avoid the curse of dimensionality, prevent overfitting, and mitigate redundant features. However, their effect on adversarial robustness across different classifiers and attack scenarios remains insufficiently explored. This study aims to analyze the effect of feature reduction techniques on the adversarial robustness of a diverse set of machine learning models under poisoning, backdoor, and universal adversarial perturbation attacks on the APT dataset. These models include support vector machine, decision tree, random forest, multi-layer perceptron, and k-nearest neighbors. The attained results are compared with scenarios where different feature reduction techniques are applied, including principal component analysis, permutation importance ranking, recursive feature elimination, and univariate mutual information. Metrics such as accuracy, F1-score, and mitigation score are employed to evaluate the effect of these techniques on adversarial robustness. The results demonstrate that permutation importance ranking and univariate mutual information generally provide the most consistent robustness improvements, while other methods exhibit more variable effects depending on the classifier and attack scenario.

papers.title: Overlooked and Underutilized: Prototypes are the Missing Piece in Tabular XAI
papers.abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) is frequently applied to high-stakes tabular data, yet the field relies heavily on feature attribution methods. While these approaches offer technical transparency, evaluating dozens of isolated features demands excessive cognitive effort from non-expert users. In this paper, we argue that prototypes remain overlooked and underutilized, and should be integrated as a complementary, intuitive gateway to auditing complex machine learning models. Although entire exemplars function as an intuitive baseline for prototype-based explanations, we highlight prototypical parts as particularly valuable for tabular data. By grouping related features into bounded subspaces, prototypical parts technically embody human-understandable concepts, replacing isolated features with cohesive semantic units. We support this integration through two primary lenses. Cognitively, these parts align with Rosch's categorization theory and Kahneman's System 1 thinking to naturally reduce cognitive load for humans. Then, we introduce a Geometric Validity Triad to conceptualize why prototypes validate the data manifold - a critical dimension often neglected by existing methods. We contend that making tabular XAI genuinely comprehensible requires shifting toward composite explanation pipelines that pair intuitive similarity-based reasoning with rigorous feature-level auditing. The paper concludes by outlining open challenges of prototype-based methods and discussing potential solutions to guide future research.

papers.title: A Homogeneous Benchmark of Exoplanet Mass-Radius Relations
papers.abstract: The mass-radius ($M$-$R$) relation is fundamental to inferring the bulk composition and internal structure of exoplanets. However, published relations remain difficult to compare directly because studies adopt different planetary samples, fitting procedures, and evaluation metrics. We construct a homogeneous, quality-controlled benchmark of 963 exoplanets with dynamically measured masses and transit radii from the NASA Exoplanet Archive. We compare empirical power laws, probabilistic models, and machine-learning (ML) regressors using point accuracy, interval coverage, and probabilistic calibration. On the full test set, a multi-feature random forest has the lowest root-mean-square error, 0.329~dex in $\log_{10} M$ versus 0.368~dex for a fitted two-parameter power law ($p = 0.007$ unadjusted; $p = 0.059$ after Holm correction across 13 comparisons). Radius-only ML models perform comparably to the single power law. In three ranges of the measured radius, several methods improve on the power law below 1.6 $R_\oplus$, but none does between 1.6 and 4 $R_\oplus$. Including stellar and orbital covariates significantly improves predictions only for low-mass planets ($M < 4.4\,M_\oplus$), although this result is sensitive to missing covariate data and weakens when the training and test sets are separated by host star. Within their calibrated radius domains, the published empirical and probabilistic relations remain highly competitive. Finally, a first-order variance decomposition shows that formal measurement uncertainties account for only $\sim$3\% of the residual variance (0.067 of 0.401~dex), and the remaining $\sim$0.396~dex arises from compositional diversity, selection effects, and model approximation error.

papers.title: Cross-Dataset Inference of Central-Satellite Classification and Host Halo Masses from Galaxy neighbours with Machine Learning
papers.abstract: The classification of galaxies as centrals or satellites gives insight into the galaxy-halo connection. This, together with halo mass estimates, can be used to connect observed galaxy populations to underlying dark matter structure. To (1) classify galaxies as centrals or satellites and (2) estimate the host halo mass for centrals, we train XGBoost models on IllustrisTNG (TNG100) galaxies, using the distances (3D or projected (2+1)D redshift space) and $M_*$ of their ten nearest neighbours. We then test the model on EAGLE to measure its robustness after applying a simple domain-alignment step that corrects for a relative shift in the $M_*$ distribution between TNG100 and EAGLE. We further augment the training data by combining feature sets from neighbour samples with varying lower $M_*$ thresholds. On the TNG100 test set, the central/satellite classifier reaches purity and completeness $=0.97$ (0.95) in 3D (projected redshift) space at the threshold where purity=completeness, and the halo-mass regressor achieves $r^2$=0.98 (0.93) when evaluated on true centrals and $r^2=0.93$ (0.93) when evaluated on inferred centrals. Applied to EAGLE after alignment, the classifier achieves purity/completeness $=0.95$ (0.95), while halo-mass inference yields $r^2=0.91$ ($0.87$) for true centrals and $r^2=0.83$ (0.77) for inferred centrals; training-data augmentation most improves the halo-mass estimation task. Satellites misclassified as centrals underpredict the true masses of host halos, especially if they are closer to a lower mass halo's central than its own host's central and/or has a significantly lower $M_*$ than its own central. These results show that survey-accessible information such as projected separations and stellar masses - combined with simulation-trained models and domain alignment - can enable reliable central identification and host halo mass estimation to an $r^2\geq 0.85$.

papers.title: Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Learning
papers.abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) has attracted increasing interest as a possible route to construct feature representations that are difficult to reproduce with classical models. However, near-term QML architectures based on trainable parametrized quantum circuits remain affected by limited hardware resources, noise, and severe optimization difficulties such as barren plateaus. In this work we propose Soft-MoQE, a Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts architecture that replaces variational quantum training with the input-dependent selection and combination of fixed quantum feature maps. The model is composed of a heterogeneous pool of non-trainable quantum circuits, each defining a distinct embedding, and a classical gating network that learns how to weight these embeddings for each data point. We benchmark Soft-MoQE on three PCA-reduced tasks: MNIST parity, MNIST 10-class, and FashionMNIST. Soft-MoQE outperforms the single best expert, the uniform average of all experts and a linear baseline, achieving task-dependent performance comparable to that of a trainable quantum neural network, without optimizing any quantum parameter and with a quantum training cost that is lower by orders of magnitude. The analysis of the class- conditioned expert usage shows that the learned routing combines a few experts for each input, with a selection that depends on the class. These results support the learned routing among fixed quantum circuits as a trainability-aware design principle for hybrid QML.

papers.title: Exploring Speaker-Aware Engagement Modeling for Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
papers.abstract: Prior work on engagement modeling in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has demonstrated substantial individual variability in behavioral features, particularly in visual modalities. In this work, we extend the literature to acoustic features in naturalistic interactions, where multiple speakers and atypical interaction patterns complicate speaker-specific analysis. We investigated whether speaker diarization improved acoustic engagement modeling during month-long, in-home socially assistive robot (SAR) interventions with seven children with ASD. We trained classical machine learning models using acoustic features extracted from diarized child and parent/caregiver audio and compared their performance with models trained on undiarized audio. Diarized audio consistently yielded higher area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) values, although these differences were not statistically significant. More importantly, the relative contributions of child and caregiver acoustic features varied across participants, indicating that the acoustic information associated with engagement was not consistent across children. These findings extend evidence of participant-level variability in ASD engagement modeling to the acoustic domain and demonstrate the feasibility of isolating speaker-specific vocalizations for studying engagement in complex, naturalistic interactions.

papers.title: Characterizing adsorption thermodynamics in carbon capture materials: an efficient first-principles approach
papers.abstract: Porous materials offer a vast design space for CO$_2$ capture, whose exploration hinges on efficient and accurate first-principles predictions of the thermodynamics governing adsorption. However, simulating isotherms and heats of adsorption using grand canonical molecular simulations is extremely computationally expensive when combined with accurate ab initio treatments of the molecular interactions, limiting screening to low-pressure uptake encoded in the Henry constant. Identifying and designing the best CO$_2$ capture materials requires a strategy that can efficiently calculate their adsorption properties using ab initio potential energy surfaces such as those now available from foundational machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs). Here we develop a neural classical density functional (cDFT) framework for carbon capture processes that allows direct calculation of adsorption isotherms from low to high loading limits of metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) without grand canonical simulations. We demonstrate the success of our approach by calculating the ab initio adsorption isotherms for over 5,000 experimentally reported MOFs. From our screening, we show how these materials can be characterized using four isotherm shapes, arising from their pore size and binding sites, which the Henry constant cannot distinguish. We show that these shapes, rather than the binding strength alone, decide which MOFs suit which process: small pores with strong binding sites for vacuum and temperature swings at low pressure, large pores with weakly binding walls for pressure swings. Finally, we identify the most promising candidates by weighing their working capacity against the energy needed for regeneration.

papers.title: Sex Differences in the Detection of Parkinson's Disease from Speech
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease in the world, and 70\% to 75\% of PD patients suffer from speech disorders at some stage. Since PD affects men more frequently than women, previous publications tend to rely on unbalanced datasets that potentially introduce sex biases into trained models. This study investigates sex differences in PD detection from speech using deep learning and traditional machine learning approaches. We evaluated speech-based PD detection using embeddings from three pre-trained speech models, combined with handcrafted acoustic features and different classifiers. Sex-specific experiments were conducted on balanced subsets of four sustained phonation datasets, controlling for sex, disease status, and, where possible, age. All recordings were obtained during a sustained phonation task. Results show that female speakers were more accurately classified than male speakers in the larger dataset. Sex-specific results show that when the models are trained on one sex, they fail to generalize to the other one. Our results highlight the importance of including sex as a variable in the development of PD detection systems.

papers.title: Surrogate Modeling and Reduced-Order Methods in Gravitational-Wave Physics and Numerical Relativity: From Spectral Representations to Adaptive Compression
papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of gravitational-wave astronomy and high-precision numerical relativity has created an acute computational bottleneck: direct numerical integration of the Einstein field equations and high-dimensional Bayesian parameter estimation require millions of waveform evaluations that cannot be sustained by traditional solvers alone. Reduced-order modeling (ROM) and surrogate techniques have emerged as foundational tools to bridge this gap, compressing high-fidelity solution manifolds into compact, rapidly evaluable representations without sacrificing physical accuracy. This perspective reviews the mathematical pillars of projection-based reduced-order modeling---including Proper Orthogonal Decomposition, greedy basis selection, and the Empirical Interpolation Method---and traces their operational impact in gravitational-wave data analysis through surrogate waveform families and Reduced-Order Quadratures. We then examine the fundamental approximation barriers posed by slow Kolmogorov n-width decay in non-stationary, transient, and strongly nonlinear regimes, showing how adaptive hp-greedy domain partitioning and multi-scale spectral compression overcome these limits. Finally, we discuss how combining certified reduced-order structures with modern scientific machine learning and sensitivity-aware quantization provides a rigorous blueprint for next-generation detectors such as LISA, Einstein Telescope, and Cosmic Explorer.

papers.title: The Long and Winding Pore: Tuning Porosity in Templated Nanoporous Carbons
papers.abstract: Disordered materials pose a recurring challenge for molecular simulation: realistic structural models are often generated through thermal protocols in which several structural descriptors emerge simultaneously and cannot easily be varied independently. Nanoporous carbons constitute a particularly relevant example: pore size, wall order, curvature, and network tortuosity generally emerge as outcomes of the thermal preparation protocol, rather than being independently prescribed structural parameters. Moreover, for practical applications, models of porous materials should ideally exhibit a percolating pore network, capable of supporting end-to-end transport of adsorbed species through the material. To this end, here we introduce a hierarchy of templating strategies, built around a common melt-quench-anneal protocol driven by a machine-learned interatomic potential for carbon, that progressively separates these variables. A rigid cylindrical template interacting with the environment through a tunable Lennard-Jones potential provides independent control over pore size and local wall organization, while leaving the structural disorder of the surrounding carbon matrix essentially unchanged. Generalizing the template to a spring-connected, tortuous backbone further allows pore geometry and curvature to be prescribed without qualitatively altering the local templating mechanism established for the straight pore. Finally, making the template mobile lets the growing carbon network reshape it in turn, which sharpens pore boundaries and allows sub-nanometer pore sizes to be targeted precisely, as needed for applications such as supercapacitor electrodes. Ultimately, this approach enables systematic studies of structure-property relationships in porous materials for applications such as energy storage, desalination and gas capture.

papers.title: On Reaction Depth and Fast Fault-Tolerant Boolean Logic
papers.abstract: Reducing runtimes of quantum applications is critical for practical viability. On quantum computers, the runtime can depend both on the speed of quantum operations and on how often the program must wait for the classical coprocessor to determine adaptive operations. Some recent approaches to reducing this overhead have focused on minimizing the "reaction depth" of a computation, informally defined as the number of times the classical coprocessor must be consulted while running a quantum program.   In this work, we formalize the notion of reaction depth. We find several subtleties in this theory. For example, we distinguish the reaction depth of a circuit from that of a circuit run, and show that the magic depth of a unitary can be higher than the reaction depth once compiled into Clifford computation and magic state injection.   We then focus on the specific case of coherent Boolean logic, a common and expensive component in quantum algorithms. We use a natural gateset for fast operations with Low-Density Parity Check (LDPC) codes, which consists of homogeneous $Z$- and $X$-type Pauli Product Measurements (PPMs), alongside a supply of Toffoli states. We prove that, using this gateset, any Boolean arithmetic circuit can be implemented on a quantum computer with constant quantum depth and constant reaction depth, at the cost of exponential space and leaving some qubits "dirty". Using the same gateset we find two efficient AutoAND circuits that require only a Toffoli state and homogeneous PPMs. We then give efficient implementations of the quantum ripple-carry adder and quantum schoolbook multiplier, which require a low number of heterogeneous PPMs for uncomputation. We find implementations competitive with the state-of-the-art despite the restricted gateset.

papers.title: Can Bandits Learn to Share a Channel? Distributed Multi-Armed Bandits for Slotted ALOHA
papers.abstract: Slotted ALOHA networks constitute a playground for research on machine learning (ML)-based channel access schemes. We consider ML agents deployed in such networks and operating under severe constraints: fully distributed (independent operation), fully online (no pre-training), aperiodic (no fixed schedule), and with no explicit coordination (no signaling). We ask whether a multi-armed bandit (MAB), a minimal reinforcement learning agent, can learn the optimal policy for a capture-free slotted ALOHA system. We evaluate several MAB algorithms on aggregate network throughput and per-node fairness. Our best-performing agent is based on a Softmax bandit, which we call SALSA (Softmax ALOHA Learning for Shared Access). SALSA learns a per-node transmission policy close to optimal, with throughput near the theoretical maximum for fair random access. We achieve performance comparable to a competing state-of-the-art solution, but without requiring a priori knowledge of the network size.

papers.title: Gradient-Based Defensive Poisoning Against System Identification Attacks on Cyber-Physical Systems
papers.abstract: AI-driven attacks learn the models of cyber-physical systems (CPS) by passively observing controller and plant signals, then use this knowledge to act covertly. Because covertness depends on the accuracy of the identified model, degrading that accuracy is a viable countermeasure. This work applies Adversarial Machine Learning as a defense, injecting small perturbations into the measurements the attacker observes to degrade an artificial neural network (ANN)-based system identification (SI) attack. The perturbations are derived from input gradients of several independently trained identification models, aggregated into a generalized perturbation, and confined to the transient regimes that carry most of the dynamic information. A sparsity parameter further restricts them to the most influential samples, with negligible cost in effectiveness. On a simulated DC motor networked control system, the proposed perturbations induce larger prediction errors than stochastic poisoning of equal root-mean-square magnitude, and the advantage widens as the magnitude grows. This limits the defense's operating range, which is intended for decoy environments such as CPS honeynets. Additional results indicate that the designed poisoning signals can also degrade N4SID-based system identification, providing evidence of their transferability beyond the ANN-based models originally targeted.

papers.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Location Encoding Methods for Species Distribution Modelling
papers.abstract: Understanding the spatial distribution of species is a key question in ecology. A variety of solutions, from statistical, traditional machine learning, through to deep learning-based methods have been proposed. These methods take sparse observations for a species of interest as input and aim to generate dense spatial outputs indicating the spatial range of the species. Orthogonal to the choice of statistical model used is the question of what input features are most informative. Thanks to recent developments, the number of options has greatly expanded, with choices spanning different climate variables, learning-based encodings, earth embedding models, or raw transformed geographic coordinates. In this work, we introduce a standardized evaluation framework and quantify the effectiveness of different location encodings in the context of species range estimation, both at the local and global scale.

papers.title: Recent developments in stochastic systems with singular dynamics -- a brief survey --
papers.abstract: Diffusions with singular drifts appear naturally in the study of certain classes of interesting particle systems. Due to the singularities involved in the equations describing them, studying their dynamics is both interesting and challenging as they fall outside of the usual regularity assumptions on the vector fields in the literature. One needs to introduce and study them with different methods, with the use of symmetric polynomials being a particularly promising approach. In this expository work, we give an overview of some models and methods, and we further explore their interactions with the areas of Multiple Loewner chains (in particular, multiple Schramm-Loewner Evolutions), the new links with Random Matrices, and the novel area of Machine Learning for Singular Dynamics.

papers.title: Morpho-Spectral Projection Analysis (MSPA) for Plant Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Plant reflectance spectroscopy across the visible, near-infrared, and shortwave infrared domain encodes foliar biochemical and anatomical traits into contiguous spectral signatures with locally differentiable structure; however, extreme inter-band collinearity and unfavorable sample-to-feature ratios challenge predictive modeling. Conventional dimensionality reduction methods routinely adopted in spectroscopy, are column-permutation invariant: they treat adjacent wavelengths as unordered tabular columns and discard the sequential differential geometry of absorption features. Here, we propose Morpho-Spectral Projection Analysis (MSPA), a supervised dimensionality reduction operator that projects contiguous spectra into a compact morpho-spectral subspace through three complementary blocks: (i) additive continuum-removed absorption depth, area, and red-edge inflection kinematics; (ii) local multi-order singular eigenmodes (0th, 1st, and 2nd derivatives) partitioned across contiguous radiative sub-windows; and (iii) global Fisher-weighted canonical subspaces regularized via trace-normalized isotropic covariance shrinkage. We validated MSPA across 8,963 spectra spanning five plant systems, coupled with six classical machine learning classifiers and four Tabular Foundation Models (TabPFN v3, TabICL v2, TabDPT v1.2, and TabFM). Despite compressing the 1,580-band spectrum by 96%, MSPA outperformed the full spectrum in 92.0% of all benchmarks and conventional reducers in 90.0% of all model-crop evaluations, raising the global mean macro-F1 from 0.7756 (full spectrum) to 0.8520, accelerating in-context inference by up to 126.5x. Designed as a self-contained spectral projection operator, the MSPA method can be directly integrated into spectroscopy workflows via the open-source code available at GitHub: https://github.com/Lucas-Osco/mspa.

papers.title: Orientation-Tunable Interfacial Thermal Conductance in Lateral MoSe2/MoS2 Heterostructures: A Deep Potential Molecular Dynamics Study
papers.abstract: Managing heat flow across interfaces in lateral 2D transition-metal dichalcogenide (TMD) heterostructures is a key challenge for next-generation nanoelectronic and optoelectronic devices. To tackle this, we trained a deep learning interatomic potential (DLP) using DeePMD-kit on density functional theory (DFT) data, then paired it with non-equilibrium molecular dynamics (NEMD) simulations to study interfacial thermal conductance (ITC) in lateral MoSe$_2$/MoS$_2$ heterostructures, considering both armchair and zigzag interface orientations. The potential we trained closely matches DFT energies, forces, and phonon dispersion relations, which confirms its reliability for thermal transport simulations. Examining cell lengths from 10 to 40 nm and extrapolating to infinite length, the armchair interface shows a higher ITC (473 MW/m$^2$K) than the zigzag interface (387 MW/m$^2$K), and the armchair interface remains higher at every length considered. Both increase further as temperature rises. At 300 K, the vibrational density of states shows greater phonon spectral overlap at the armchair interface than at the zigzag interface. Together, these results offer a solid machine-learning framework for studying heat transport in lateral TMD heterostructures, and identify interface orientation as an effective means of controlling heat dissipation at these junctions.

papers.title: Chemistry by Design (CbyD): A Machine-Readable Dataset of Expert-Curated Total Synthesis Routes
papers.abstract: Chemistry by Design (CbyD) is an open-access educational database of published total syntheses launched in 2011. It was designed to help students and practitioners learn organic reactions and synthetic strategies by depicting every step of published natural product and drug syntheses. Motivated by advances in machine learning for organic synthesis and by requests from academic and industrial researchers, we present a machine-readable version of CbyD for use in cheminformatics and computer-aided synthesis planning (CASP). The released dataset (v2026.11) contains 3,502 routes comprising 56,640 reactions toward 2,902 unique targets. Compared with patent-derived datasets, CbyD reactions are more complex, more frequently change stereochemistry, and are less likely to be covered by patent-derived reaction templates, and CbyD routes are longer and more convergent than those in commonly used CASP benchmarks. We also analyze how molecular complexity changes along these routes and identify transformations associated with large complexity increases. The CbyD dataset will be expanded through versioned public releases that incorporate new routes and community-contributed corrections.

papers.title: Machine-learned potentials for iron oxides at extreme conditions
papers.abstract: Reliable phase stability requires accurate relative free energies, which small force errors alone do not guarantee. We develop atomic-cluster-expansion potentials for five iron oxides from Fe$_2$O to Fe$_2$O$_3$, covering crystalline and liquid states at 140--260\,GPa and 1000--11000\,K, with electronic and ionic temperatures matched. Force-dominated training leaves systematic energy offsets between structure families of up to 41\,meV/atom that persist despite additional training data. Stronger energy weighting and weaker regularization largely remove these offsets, while converged k-point sampling prevents further composition-dependent biases. The final potentials achieve held-out energy errors of 2.0--5.5\,meV/atom and first-order free-energy errors within 3.4\,meV/atom for liquids at 5000--9000\,K. However, an untrained NiAs-type FeO phase exhibits a free-energy error of 57\,meV/atom despite a low extrapolation grade. These results show that reliable phase-diagram calculations require control of relative energy offsets and explicit free-energy validation of every competing phase.

papers.title: Single-Controller Teleoperation and Multimodal Dataset Generation for a Mobile Manipulator
papers.abstract: Robot learning systems require synchronized, high-quality demonstrations that combine visual, proprioceptive, and action data. However, collecting such datasets with mobile manipulators is often slowed down by fragmented teleoperation interfaces and manual post-processing workflows. This paper presents an integrated framework for teleoperated multimodal data collection on a Clearpath Dingo-O mobile base equipped with a Kinova Gen3 Lite manipulator and an Intel RealSense RGB-D camera. The framework combines single-controller operation of the base, arm, and recording process with an automated ROS-based pipeline for data capture, image-quality filtering, temporal synchronization, visualization, and export to machine-learning-ready Zarr datasets. We validate the system on a pick-and-place mobile-manipulation task in which the robot transports a bottle between two surfaces. The results show that the unified controller supports complete task execution and recording without external commands, while the data pipeline produces synchronized datasets for short demonstrations and identifies corrupted visual frames. The proposed framework provides a practical basis for producing structured demonstrations for robot-learning research.

papers.title: Drift-Aware Explainable Prioritization for Windows PE Malware Forensic Triage with Semantic Consistency Checks
papers.abstract: Forensic investigators must decide which suspicious files to examine first. Machine-learning (ML) and deep-learning (DL) malware detectors usually return a bare score that neither explains why a file deserves attention nor signals when changing data make the model unreliable. We present a framework for Windows Portable Executable (PE) malware forensic triage that works only on pre-extracted static features and never executes malware. A calibrated maliciousness score sets each file's triage priority, and a per-sample feature attribution explains the prediction. A per-sample consistency score measures whether the top attributed features agree with documented behaviors from the Malware Behavior Catalog (MBC) and MITRE Adversarial Tactics, Techniques & Common Knowledge (ATT&CK), where the available features support such interpretation. Conformal evaluation and statistical distribution tests flag drift. Each file receives one investigator-oriented triage output. The evaluation protocol, specified before testing, uses a time-ordered split of EMBER2024 as the primary dataset and BODMAS for family disjoint checks, and compares every component with simple baselines on predictive performance, prioritization effectiveness, explanation quality and robustness over time.

papers.title: Advancing mixed-effects random forests for predictions based on multi-cohort data
papers.abstract: Pooling longitudinal cohorts can extend age coverage and improve long-term health predictions, but cohort heterogeneity complicate estimation and prediction. Mixed-effects machine learning (ME-ML) combines flexible machine learning methods with mixed-effect models to account for correlated observations, yet these ME-ML methods are limited in their applicability in complex settings such as multi-cohort data. We propose a multi-cohort mixed-effects random forest (MERFmulti-cohort) for improving predictions of individual health trajectories beyond the observed period. The method extends standard MERF through (i) better separation of population-level and subject-specific variation, (ii) flexibility in correcting systematic discrepancies in fixed-effects estimates to improve covariance parameter estimation, and (iii) flexible specification of random-effects and residual variance-covariance structures. We evaluate MERFmulti-cohort against linear regression, linear mixed models, random forests, and standard MERF in simulations and four real-data scenarios predicting BMI z-scores in children and adolescents. In simulations, MERFmulti-cohort improves covariance parameter estimation across several covariance structures while achieving prediction accuracy comparable to standard MERF. Predictive gains are most obvious when residual variances vary across study waves. In real-data applications, MERFmulti-cohort improves predictive accuracy relative to MERF by flexibly capturing complex patterns and accommodating cohort heterogeneity. Pooling similar cohorts covering extended age coverage can improve future individual-level predictions if the heterogeneity in multi-cohort data is adequately accounted for.

papers.title: Harmonic Circuit: Chord Progression Lies in a Sparse Principal Information Flow in Symbolic Music Models
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) seeks to decode neural network computations into human-understandable logic. A core methodology in MI is circuit discovery: identifying the information flow in sub-networks that drive specific model behaviors. While circuit discovery has matured within Natural Language Processing (NLP), the interpretable circuits in music models remain largely unexplored. In this work, we identify a music-functional circuit within two symbolic music generative models: ChatMusician and MuPT. The music function we consider is the prediction of the terminal tonic root in a classical harmonic progression pattern $I \ldots V \rightarrow I$. We use the Auto-Emergence algorithm to extract a principal sparse sub-network as the identified circuit. Validation via causal intervention confirms that this identified circuit is a primary driver of harmonic progression behaviors in the symbolic music models. To our knowledge, this represents the first systematic circuit-discovery study conducted within the music domain. Our demo page is available at: https://ukiyo23rui.github.io/auto-emergence-demo/.

papers.title: Predicting Process-Level Behavior: A Benchmarking Study
papers.abstract: Predictive process monitoring (PPM) typically forecasts the future of individual process instances, hence operating on trace level. Process managers, however, typically operate on process level, e.g., when assigning staff or calculating KPIs. The question is how well such process-level managerial decisions are supported by existing approaches, given that PPM research has so far not focused on process-level predictions. We answer this question through a comprehensive benchmarking study of two process-level prediction tasks: concurrent trace prediction and average throughput time prediction. Across synthetic and real-life event logs, we compare statistical and machine-learning-based methods, foundation models, business process simulation, and, importantly, established trace-level PPM approaches, aggregating their predictions to the process-level. We assess which modeling paradigms are most suitable for predicting process-level behavior and whether existing trace-level PPM can be effectively repurposed for this task. Our results show substantial variation in performance across approaches. Notably, aggregated trace-level predictions cause errors to compound on process-level, reducing accuracy and highlighting process-level prediction as a distinct predictive task that warrants dedicated research.

papers.title: Orbital-weighted learning for transition metal complexes
papers.abstract: Frontier orbital energies are key to the description of molecular light-matter interaction and pose a challenge both for electronic structure calculations and for machine learning approaches, especially for transition metal complexes (TMC). These are highly relevant since the gap between the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) is in the range of visible light. For TMCs, gap position and magnitude are determined by the metal center, its coordination and ligand identity. Since the systems exhibit a wide range of charge and spin states, frontier orbital energies can only be predicted with machine learning models that explicitly incorporate spin and charge. In this work, we show that a semi-empirical orbital population as a weight rather than a feature can increase efficiency for both physics-based and neural-network-based atomic representations. Because orbital populations are highly sensitive to both charge and spin, they offer a general pathway to render existing geometry-based machine learning representations useful for orbital energies. On TMC datasets, our approach reduces the required training data by up to 95 %, and improves physics-based representations to almost match the accuracy of pre-trained neural network representations at 12% of the inference compute cost. This greatly reduces the data and compute requirements to accurately model frontier orbitals in TMCs

papers.title: ScaleBench: An Extensible and Reproducible Experimental Platform for Kubernetes Autoscaling Research
papers.abstract: Autoscaling enables cloud-native applications to meet their SLOs by dynamically adjusting computational resources at runtime. Recent research has explored a broad range of advanced autoscaling approaches, including rule-based, optimisation-based, and machine learning-based techniques, to address the limitations of traditional resource management strategies in cloud-native environments. Despite significant advances, a considerable gap remains between academic innovations and their practical adoption in real-world environments. For instance, Kubernetes deployments commonly rely on the reactive, CPU-based Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, limiting the adoption of more advanced autoscaling approaches. Recent studies have investigated challenges such as autoscaler configuration and reproducible performance evaluation; however, the practical deployment, integration complexity, and operational overhead of research-based autoscalers in Kubernetes environments have received limited attention. To address this gap, we present ScaleBench, a native Kubernetes experimental platform to enable extensible and reproducible evaluation of autoscaling solutions. Unlike existing approaches, ScaleBench integrates autoscalers as native Kubernetes components, allowing researchers to assess not only scaling performance but also deployment characteristics and integration requirements within realistic cloud-native environments. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ScaleBench by evaluating multiple autoscaling approaches through a case study. The results highlight its capability to support systematic, repeatable, and practical assessment of Kubernetes autoscaling approaches.

papers.title: Exploring Daily Emotional Well-Being through Personalized Data Analysis
papers.abstract: This project analysed daily emotional well-being from a personalized perspective using records of emotional states and contextual information derived from daily life. It was based on the idea that well-being is not a fixed value, but varies from day to day, and can be better understood in relation to individual context and behaviour. The work is framed within the field of Data Science and focuses on emotional states at an individual level. The project focused on constructing an integrated daily dataset from multiple personal data sources and analysing emotional states. The distributions of emotional variables, their temporal evolution and the differences between users were studied, together with their variability over time. Personality and well-being questionnaires were also incorporated as stable references to better contextualize daily emotional results. A simple personalized recommendation approach was then developed by comparing similar days within each user, exploring how past contextual conditions relate to differences in the user's emotional state. Finally, machine learning techniques were used to evaluate whether daily contextual information contains signals that help distinguish between different types of days relative to a person's usual well-being. The project adopted an applied approach, with an exploratory scope focused on understanding patterns rather than building a fully predictive system. The results showed that emotional well-being is very personal and changes from day to day. General models had limited value, while personalized approaches captured these differences much better, highlighting the importance of analysing each person on their own terms.

papers.title: QuFrame: Pauli Frame Tracking for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Control
papers.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires continuous quantum error correction (QEC) to suppress physical noise. While Clifford-only workloads can defer corrections to software post-processing, universal computation breaks this paradigm: executing non-Clifford gates via magic-state gadgets introduces hard, real-time control-flow dependencies on error-corrected measurements. Consequently, the controller must extract syndromes, decode them, and update the Pauli frame in real time, closing the entire QEC loop within a strict $1\,μ\text{s}$ cycle. However, prior proposals on Pauli frame tracking remain largely theoretical, leaving the microarchitectural bottlenecks of tracking, resolving, and synchronizing frame updates across distributed control pipelines unaddressed. To this end, we present QuFrame, a control microarchitecture for real-time Pauli frame tracking that closes the QEC loop within $1\,μ\text{s}$ while sustaining QPU-rate throughput. By introducing QuFrameISA, we cleanly decouple instruction execution from continuous Pauli frame management. Execution is distributed across per-qubit Instruction Resolution Engines (IREs) that resolve instructions against the frame via a single table lookup, while a Pauli Frame Management Unit enables independent, lock-free concurrent commits. To strictly guarantee the $1\,μ\text{s}$ deadline, QuFrame pairs an asynchronous primary decoder with an on-chip fallback decoder that resolves in $144\,\text{ns}$, natively reconciling divergent updates in hardware without degrading logical error rates.

papers.title: Beyond Corpus-Driven Imitation: Evolving Musical Mindsets in the Agentic Orchestra via Quantum Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: This paper presents a framework for computer-aided music composition and performance based on quantum reinforcement learning and multi-agent interaction. We introduce the agentic orchestra, where musical agents evolve distinct mindsets through trial-and-error engagement with a musical environment, rather than through training on large datasets. The agents are implemented as parameterised quantum circuits. They evolve distinct compositional behaviours, referred to as mindsets. This enables the exploration of musical decision spaces using quantum superposition and entanglement within a hybrid quantum-classical loop. We present two complementary agent architectures: atomistic agents, which process pitch and rhythm independently, and holistic agents, which handle pitch and duration as unified note events. Mindsets are shaped through musically grounded reward functions, which can be combined and weighted to develop different mindsets across agents. The resulting system positions quantum computing agents less as autonomous composers and more as adaptive musical partners, each developing its own musical personality through interaction rather than imitation. Demonstrations show how agents generalise their learned behaviour to previously unseen material, operating in interactive and offline batch modes using MIDI-encoded music. While quantum computers are still in development, experiments conducted on IBM quantum hardware confirmed that musically meaningful learning is achievable with existing quantum computers. For composers and performers, the agentic orchestra opens new possibilities for emergent, process-oriented musical creativity, offering a scalable foundation for quantum computer-aided music composition as quantum computing technology continues to advance.

papers.title: Element-Wise Femoral Stress Prediction: A Hybrid Graph Neural Network Surrogate for Finite Element Analysis
papers.abstract: Hip fractures represent a significant clinical challenge because they cause excess disability and mortality, and have a growing incidence in aging populations, as bone fragility increases. Although finite element analysis (FEA) provides biomechanical assessment of femoral strength, its clinical applicability is mainly limited by high computational cost. Conventional machine learning (ML) approaches have been explored as surrogate models for FEA; predictions are fast but fail to capture the spatial and topological structure of finite element meshes. To address these limitations, this study proposes a hybrid Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based framework for femoral stress prediction using graph-structured finite element modeling (FEM) data. The proposed GCN-SAGE-Residual architecture combines graph convolution, neighborhood aggregation, and residual learning to model spatial dependencies and stress propagation across mesh elements. We systematically evaluated 14 models in a primary comparison, spanning classical ML methods and baseline GNN architectures, complemented by a targeted architectural ablation that isolates the contribution of each component of the proposed design. Evaluation results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid architecture achieves the strongest predictive performance among all evaluated models. The proposed hybrid model achieves the best performance with an R^2 score of 0.8022 and mean absolute error of 2.879 MPa, highlighting the importance of incorporating mesh topology in biomechanical prediction tasks. The proposed framework provides a scalable and computationally efficient alternative for FEM-based orthopedic analyses and fracture risk assessment. The code is publicly available on GitHub.

papers.title: Search for Heavy Charged Higgs Bosons in Boosted Top and Bottom Quark Final States at a 1.4 TeV Future Lepton Collider
papers.abstract: The discovery potential for heavy charged Higgs bosons $H^\pm$ decaying into a top-bottom quark pair is investigated at a future $e^+e^-$ collider operating at $\sqrt{s}=1.4~\mathrm{TeV}$. The study considers charged Higgs masses between 200 and 600 GeV within all four Yukawa types of the two-Higgs-doublet model (2HDM). The boosted $tb$ final state is explored using complementary cut-based and machine-learning analyses based on boosted decision trees (BDT). The expected signal significance and sensitivity contours in the $(m_{H^\pm},\tanβ)$ plane are obtained for each Yukawa type. The resulting sensitivity extends to regions of the 2HDM parameter space beyond the projected reach of the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC), demonstrating the complementary potential of a future high-energy lepton collider to probe heavy charged Higgs bosons.

papers.title: Stochastic Optimisation for Scalable Ptychographic Image Reconstruction
papers.abstract: X-ray ptychography is a lensless coherent diffraction imaging technique capable of high spatial resolution, in which an image is reconstructed by solving a large-scale inverse problem from highly redundant far-field diffraction measurements acquired under overlapping illumination. Whilst the measurement redundancy created by overlapping illumination is essential for reconstruction fidelity, it leads to computational and memory demands that scale poorly with object size and target resolution when using conventional reconstruction algorithms. This work proposes a ptychographic reconstruction framework that reduces peak memory usage and time to convergence by leveraging stochastic optimisation techniques developed for large-scale machine learning. Specifically, the framework employs stochastic gradient descent with a decaying step size that progressively reduces the effect of gradient noise, referred to here as variance reduction (VR), with gradients that agree with automatic differentiation, to optimise the ptychographic forward model using randomly sampled subsets of diffraction measurements. For an experimental dataset of 200,000 diffraction patterns of $128\times128$ pixels, VR is demonstrated to require $65\%$ of the peak GPU memory and $22\%$ of the reconstruction time of the established maximum-likelihood (ML) algorithm. The VR framework incorporates the Poisson maximum-likelihood formulation and partial coherence within a unified and extensible optimisation setting. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the framework achieves reconstruction quality visually comparable to established methods, with lower peak GPU memory and a shorter time

papers.title: Large-Scale Tensor Trace-Ratio Problem: Randomized Algorithm and Sparse Multilinear Discriminant Analysis via Closed-Form Solution
papers.abstract: Trace-ratio optimization problems from high-dimensional tensor data appear across numerous research domains including machine learning, signal processing, as well as pattern recognition. Up to now, analytical closed-form expressions remain unavailable for tensor trace-ratio tasks; prevailing techniques mostly adopt inner-outer iterative schemes to tackle such optimization tasks. However, when dealing with high-dimensional tensor data sets, existing multilinear discriminant analysis methods often encounter limitations such as heavy computational costs, insufficient memory space, and interference from redundant features. This paper yields two core contributions.First, we present a closed-form solution under the full row rank condition, and construct a randomized solver targeting large-scale tensor trace-ratio optimization. In contrast to prior approaches, the devised algorithm achieves substantial computational speedup.Its core mechanism is to reformulate the original large-scale tensor trace-ratio optimization into a tensor least-squares formulation, instead of the much more complicated (generalized) tensor eigenproblems. We derive theoretical error-bound results which verify the reliability of the newly developed algorithm. Second, we build a sparse multilinear discriminant analysis model leveraging the above closed-form result combined with tensor \ell_{2,0}-norm regularization, and propose a sparse multilinear discriminant method for tensor feature selection. The sparse method can identify key discriminative features from high-dimensional data and suppress redundant information. Comprehensive numerical evaluations are conducted over multiple publicly available real-world benchmarks.The proposed methods demonstrate significant advantages in computational efficiency and scalability for large-scale problems, while achieving competitive classification accuracy on some datasets.

papers.title: Monitoring Unplanned Construction Using Satellite Change Detection
papers.abstract: Cities need land for homes, shops, roads, and public services. New construction changes that land. It can harm natural areas and water bodies, add to waste, and strain public services. NITI Aayog's 2021 report stated that 65% of 7,933 urban settlements in India had no master plan. That number tells us about planning coverage at the time. It does not tell us whether any single building was authorised. Artificial intelligence, which lets computers learn patterns from data, can help find physical changes by comparing satellite images taken on different dates. We test simple methods on two public datasets from outside India. First, we turn each image into a set of numbers using a pretrained neural network, a model already trained to recognise patterns in images. We feed those numbers to standard machine-learning classifiers that predict land categories and physical changes. The methods reach about 95 percent accuracy at spotting built-up land and about 83 percent accuracy at saying whether a small pair of images shows change, where each pair gets one label. We also train a small neural network on a standard change-detection benchmark. Separately, we run a preliminary descriptive check on an Agra sample of 48 patches, 7 of them positive. The results show that satellite images carry information about physical change. They do not show whether construction was planned or permitted.

papers.title: Gradient Blindness in Adaptive Architecture Search for IQP Born Machines
papers.abstract: Instantaneous quantum polynomial (IQP) Born machines learn a probability distribution from data with a circuit of commuting gates that a classical computer trains at hundreds of qubits. Adaptive algorithms grow a sparse circuit from a small seed by adding in every round the candidate gates with the largest loss gradient. Such algorithms never add a candidate whose gradient vanishes, so the choice of seed decides which circuits they can reach. Here we show that a candidate gate has a nonzero gradient for some angles of the circuit exactly when its generator is the sum of an odd number of linearly independent generators already in the circuit. The common seed of one-qubit gates therefore never adds a gate on an even number of qubits, which exact gradients on 12 qubits confirm. A seed of one-qubit gates plus the edges of the Chow-Liu tree sees every candidate, and its circuits match the full circuits on 12 and 16 qubits with 10 to 13 percent of their parameters. At 484 qubits, a heredity pool keeps the search over higher-order gates feasible, and the circuits grown from this seed reach a lower test loss than the dense two-body circuit with 6 percent of its parameters, although the higher-order gates add no gain.

papers.title: Target-Clamped Contrastive Learning in Nonlinear Resistive Networks with Monotone Elements
papers.abstract: In the pursuit of energy-efficient hardware for machine learning, nonlinear resistive networks trained via local learning rules are emerging as promising alternatives to digital neural networks. Learning in these physical systems is often achieved with Equilibrium Propagation (EP), which compares a "free" state to a "nudged" target-driven state to perform gradient descent on an objective defined by an explicit cost function. In contrast, Target-Clamped Contrastive Learning (TCCL) "clamps" output nodes directly to exact target values, performing gradient descent on an implicit contrastive function - an objective whose properties have long remained unknown. Focusing on nonlinear networks composed of resistors with monotonically increasing current-voltage characteristics (such as Ohmic resistors and diodes), our contribution is twofold. First, we establish rigorous convergence guarantees for TCCL. We prove that the contrastive function is convex for nonlinear resistive networks without hidden nodes, and demonstrate that this property does not hold in general for the objective function optimized by EP. For these networks, TCCL converges to a global minimum of the contrastive function under suitable assumptions on the learning rate. In the presence of hidden nodes, the contrastive function is not convex, but we show that TCCL still converges to a stationary point on a subsequence. We also reveal cases where such stationary points are global minimizers of the contrastive function. Second, we characterize the representational capacity of these circuits. We establish a novel function approximation theorem demonstrating that any continuous, monotonically non-decreasing, and shift-equivariant function can be approximated to arbitrary precision, proving that these properties are the sole limitations on the network's computational expressivity.

papers.title: Machine learning interatomic potentials and orientational defects in polymers
papers.abstract: Photopolymerization of acrylated epoxidized soybean oil (AESO) is a convenient model of a self-organizing process in a soft, bio-based material: ultraviolet light starts a free-radical chain reaction, the growing network releases heat, and the mobility of molecular groups changes on several time scales at once. We follow this process from two sides. Experimentally, the real and imaginary parts of the dielectric permittivity of an AESO:VDM (1:0.5) mixture with 3 mol% of the photoinitiator DMPA were recorded at 500-5000 Hz under an intermittent on/off illumination protocol, and the resulting time series were analysed with a sliding-window Shannon entropy and the Grassberger-Procaccia correlation integral. Both measures show that short light pulses at the start of curing trigger strongly correlated, collective relaxation, which fades as the network forms, leaving only localized reorientations active. We describe these reorientations as orientational defects and quantify their energetics with the MACE-OFF23 machine learning interatomic potential, using relaxed dihedral scans of five rotational modes ($α$, $α/β$, $β$, $γ$, $δ$) of an AESO fragment. Compared with density functional theory (DFT) reference profiles, MACE reproduces the shape of all five profiles (Pearson $r=0.95$-$0.98$) and the hierarchy of barriers - from 2.9 eV for the constrained main-chain rotation, through 0.54-0.81 eV for the acrylate rotations, to 0.16-0.18 eV for the methyl and 0.06 eV for the hydroxyl rotation - while underestimating the barrier heights by 3-20%. A simple Arrhenius estimate shows that the acrylate rotations are the modes closest to the frequency window of the dielectric measurement.

papers.title: Uncovering the Structural, Electronic, and Electrostatic Landscapes of SrTiO$_3$ Grain Boundaries via Grand Canonical Monte Carlo with a Machine-Learning Interatomic Potential
papers.abstract: Grain boundaries in perovskites exhibit a rich variety of electronic, polar and magnetic properties, yet identifying their atomic structures and compositions remains challenging. Here, we combine the Grand Canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) method with a universal machine-learning interatomic potential to explore the coupled compositional and structural phase space of $Σ$5(310)[001] SrTiO$_3$ grain boundaries. The resulting chemical potential phase diagram identifies ten stable structures belonging to four motif families: large Sr kite, small Sr kite, incomplete Sr large kite, and Ti-rich structures. Extending the GCMC method to the Sigma5(210)[001] and Sigma17(410)[001] grain boundaries reveals how grain boundary plane and inclination angle influence the competition between small- and large-kite motifs. Density functional theory calculations of the predicted Sigma5(310)[001] grain boundaries show that the composition and atomic structure strongly govern the spatial distribution of conduction and valence band edge states, interfacial band alignment, and carrier localization. Four distinct electronic regimes emerge: localized electron-doped, delocalized electron-doped, insulating, and hole-attracting states. Our electrostatics analysis reveals the coexistence of the short-range electric fields at the reconstructed GB core associated with local atomic density and bonding, and the longer-range fields outside the core arising from the space charge. These fields can also couple to local polar distortions and generate composition-dependent polarization patterns. These results establish an efficient framework for exploring oxide perovskite grain boundary structures and reveal how stoichiometry and atomic reconstruction couple to electronic structure, electrostatics, and local polarization, providing a route toward predictive grain boundary engineering in functional perovskites.

papers.title: A GPU-Native Nested Sampling Framework for Finite-Temperature Materials Modelling with Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
papers.abstract: Modern equivariant machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have dramatically improved the accuracy of and the scales accessible to atomistic simulation, yet the thermodynamic sampling methods needed to turn those potentials into finite-temperature phase stability predictions have not kept pace computationally. We present the GPU-native, massively parallel nested sampling framework JAXRENS, implemented on top of JAX, which removes the practical bottlenecks preventing atomistic nested sampling from being combined with state-of-the-art MLIPs. The framework provides distributed multi-GPU execution, vectorised ensembles of walkers, and direct interoperability with modern force fields. We demonstrate the highly beneficial scaling of JAXRENS on hardware accelerators, and apply it to the simulation of the ZnS phase diagram based on a MACE foundation model, a procedure previously computationally inaccessible. Despite requiring in the order of 10^10 model evaluations, the final converged simulation completed within six days on four GPUs, marking an important step towards routine, first-principles-quality predictions of finite-temperature phase stability using machine-learned interatomic potentials.

papers.title: Attention Is Not Relevance: Challenging the Causality of Attention in Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Attention has become one of the most widely adopted solutions for estimating the relevance of surrounding objects and interpreting an autonomous vehicle's driving decisions. However, its ability to capture the causal impact of individual input elements on an AI model's output has long been discussed in the literature, particularly in the Natural Language Processing (NLP) domain. This work brings this discussion into the autonomous driving domain by analyzing the accuracy of attention in estimating the impact of an input object on an autonomous vehicle's driving, i.e., its relevance. To this end, we compare different attention-based relevance estimation methods against a causal reference of object relevance obtained through counterfactual analysis. We perform our analysis on more than 80,000 synthetic driving scenes using an autonomous vehicle based on PlanT 2.0, a state-of-the-art Transformer-based model for object-level planning. Results show that attention provides a correlational rather than causal indication of object relevance. Attention-based relevance estimation methods do not consistently identify all relevant objects and tend to incorrectly classify as relevant objects with little or no impact on the vehicle's driving. In particular, results show that attention can effectively identify relevant objects in simple single-lane, straight-road scenarios, but its accuracy degrades in more complex settings, such as multi-lane roads and intersections. These findings highlight the limitations of attention as a proxy for object relevance, calling for novel methods able to accurately capture the causal impact of individual objects on the vehicle's driving and distinguish it from correlational associations.

papers.title: Is It Worth Collecting Additional Covariates?
papers.abstract: In many studies, basic covariates are routinely recorded at negligible cost, whereas acquiring additional covariates requires expensive or time-consuming procedures. Thus, a natural question is whether it is worth to collecting these additional covariates. Using the reduction in prediction interval width as criterion, we evaluate and test the gain brought by the additional covariates and hence answer this question. We consider the gain both marginally and conditionally on the observable characteristics. The conditional formulation captures subpopulation heterogeneity and supports individualized data acquisition decisions. To avoid restrictive parametric assumptions, we adopt a model-free framework that accommodates flexible nonparametric or machine learning methods. We propose an efficient influence function based method, with proven theoretical properties to achieve our purpose under mild nuisance convergence rates. Interestingly, we find the natural conformal prediction based method cannot achieve the same purpose: It fails in the marginal case and imposes much more stringent or even infeasible requirement on the nuisance parameter estimation procedures. We demonstrate the superior finite-sample performance of the proposed procedures through simulations and real data applications.

papers.title: Topological Quantum Reservoir Computing
papers.abstract: Scaling universal quantum computation and implementing quantum machine learning with protected logical qubits remain challenging. To harness the computational potential of existing fault-tolerant quantum platforms, we introduce topological quantum reservoir computing, a novel approach using protected degrees of freedom for storage and the host system's intrinsic dynamics for information processing. Using a one-dimensional Kitaev chain, we show how long-lived Majorana edge modes and fast bulk responses support these complementary functions within the same many-body system. We identify the tradeoffs governing access to protected memory and show how matched interfaces enable programmable writing and interactions enable autonomous information consolidation from the bulk to the edge. These mechanisms improve performance on tasks requiring long-term retention of temporal information. Our results establish topology as a new resource for quantum reservoir computing and open a route toward near-term quantum computing and quantum machine learning.

papers.title: OMNIS+: Semantic RAN Slicing and Quantization for Dynamic Split Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Edge computing enables resource-constrained devices to execute machine learning (ML) applications via task offloading, with radio access network (RAN) slicing playing a crucial role in provisioning joint communication and computing resources. However, existing RAN slicing frameworks rely on static computing models, limiting their ability to exploit dynamic semantic data representations enabled by modern neural architectures. To address this limitation, we propose OMNIS+, a semantic RAN slicing framework for multi-cell edge computing built upon a new generation of dynamic split neural models. OMNIS+ incorporates dynamic neural compression paired with adaptive quantization for task offloading, providing a versatile decision space across communication payload and compute dimensions. We leveraged a novel ``box'' quantization scheme that markedly enhances resilience to transmission bit errors across diverse compression rates. Considering partial system observability and distinct node objectives, we formulate two interdependent optimization problems: (i)~mobile devices (MDs) maximize inference accuracy under quality-of-service (QoS) and queue-stability constraints by jointly adapting dynamic split deep neural network (DNN) branches and cell association; and (ii)~each edge server (ES) allocates bandwidth, graphics processing unit (GPU) frequency, and modulation and coding scheme (MCS) to maximize the max--min inference accuracy among associated MDs under cell capacity limits. We solve these problems using a multi-agent distributed optimization framework, where MDs act as causal contextual multi-armed bandit (MAB) agents under backlog-aware Lyapunov control, while each ES executes resource allocation via block coordinate descent (BCD). Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, OMNIS+ reduces the QoS violation probability by up to 1.75 while achieving a better accuracy--violation trade-off.

papers.title: Faster than square-root run-time in adiabatic quantum algorithms for Exact Cover 3
papers.abstract: By intertwining ideas from sequential and adiabatic quantum computing, we propose a quantum algorithm for the problem class Exact Cover 3, which is a sub-class of 3-satisfiability (3-SAT) problems and NP (nondeterministic polynomial time) complete. We find a quantum run-time which is significantly faster than the square-root run-time $N\to N^{1/2}$ of the Grover algorithm. Depending on the structure of the problem (e.g., connectivity of clauses), the run-time scaling may range from approximately third root $N\to N^{1/3}$ to nearly fourth root $N\to N^{1/4}$, possibly even faster.
